extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor theory, playwrights/comic artists, and readers of philosophical criticism on comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical/critical analysis of what makes things laughable, focusing on bodily gestures, repetition, disguise, formality, and the transformation of persons into mechanical or object-like images. Useful for theorists, playwrights, comic artists, and critics who want principled criteria for producing or evaluating comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Something mechanical encrusted on the living
rubrics_metrics.description: Central image: the comic often arises from 'something mechanical encrusted on the living' — a machine-like element imposed on a living human or social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core organizing principle: identify where artificial/mechanical/formulaic elements are superposed on living flexibility. The essay treats this theme as a branching source for multiple comic effects; use it to derive repetition, disguise, formality, objectification, and institutional automatism examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitudes, gestures and movements: machine-likeness proportionally laughable
rubrics_metrics.description: THE ATTITUDES, GESTURES AND MOVEMENTS OF THE HUMAN BODY ARE LAUGHABLE IN EXACT PROPORTION AS THAT BODY REMINDS US OF A MERE MACHINE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drawings, performances, or descriptions by how clearly and subtly they allow the viewer to 'see a man as a jointed puppet.' Comic artists should make the machine-suggestion both distinct and yet still embedded in a living person; the better the fit between the image of person and machine, the stronger the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition / automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures or movements that repeat identically create the impression of an automatism and therefore provoke laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for recurring, predictable movements (a speaker's repeated head-turn, a recurring physical tic). If an action ceases to change and is expected, it reads as mechanical rather than alive. In performance and writing, deliberate repetition can be used to produce comic automatism; avoid repetition that feels dead or unmotivated unless the aim is to show mechanicalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation exposes automatism and increases laughability
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is laughable because it highlights the mechanical uniformity in a person's gestures; 'To imitate any one is to bring out the element of automatism he has allowed to creep into his person.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody and mimicry should aim to make the gesture appear intentionally mechanical (e.g., link it to a simple mechanical occupation like sawing or tugging a bell-rope). Imitation becomes funnier when it not only copies but also reinterprets the gesture as part of a mechanical task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity plus subtlety of the machine-person overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: The suggestion that a person is machine-like must be both clear and subtle: clear enough to be perceived, subtle enough that the person still appears alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect is maximized when the audience can distinctly perceive both the human and the mechanical image simultaneously. Over-clarification (pure caricature) or over-obscurity (no machine impression) weakens the effect; the balance is key to consummate comic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity (loss of gracefulness) as the comic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is more about rigidity than ugliness; it is a loss of gracefulness when matter dulls the outward life of the soul that produces comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing comedy, prioritize detection of stiffness, immobility, or fixedness (in movement, posture, or expression) rather than simply unattractiveness. Comic strategies should contrast gracefulness with rigid, stereotyped form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise and fashion as sources of comic incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: A man in disguise (or one perceived as disguised) is comic; fashions/clothes become laughable when they are seen as disguises or when continuity of custom is broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effects arise when costume/clothing or changed appearance creates a perceptual discontinuity (e.g., someone dressing in outdated fashion or surprising hair/skin coloration). Note that routine familiarity often deadens the comic quality; a sudden dissolution of continuity revives it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masquerade of nature and society (derived disguise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any appearance of nature or society masquerading—i.e., artificially tampered-with nature or ready-made stereotyped social forms—can be comic, though often faintly unless brought closer to the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imagery that contrasts a natural/living original with an obviously manufactured or formulaic imitation (e.g., artificial waterfalls, manufactured virtues). Emphasize the artificiality to strengthen comic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremony and formality: isolating form from matter yields comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The ceremonial side of social life contains a latent comic element; if one isolates the ceremonial/formal aspect from its serious matter, it becomes comic (e.g., prize-distribution, solemn court sitting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce comedy, draw attention to the mechanical rituals and formulas of social institutions while neglecting or downplaying the substantive purpose they are meant to serve. Formalities presented as ends in themselves are ripe for ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional/administrative automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: When human regulation or bureaucratic routine usurps natural or moral laws, the resulting mechanical application is comic (examples: officers asking wreck survivors 'if they had anything to declare').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight the mismatch between rigid rules/procedures and human situations; present regulations acting 'with inexorable fatality' as though they were laws of nature to elicit comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: The body taking precedence of the soul (physical intrusion into moral contexts)
rubrics_metrics.description: ANY INCIDENT IS COMIC THAT CALLS OUR ATTENTION TO THE PHYSICAL IN A PERSON WHEN IT IS THE MORAL SIDE THAT IS CONCERNED (e.g., a speaker sneezing at a pathetic moment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic occurrences often pivot on an abrupt shift of attention from moral/intellectual concerns to bodily/material ones. In dramatic writing, avoid bodily details in tragic contexts unless you intend a comic undermining; use such intrusions deliberately to produce laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner outrunning matter / profession replaced by formality
rubrics_metrics.description: When manner, rituals, or professional trappings become more important than the underlying purpose ('the manner seeking to outdo the matter; the letter aiming at ousting the spirit'), it produces comedy (e.g., doctors who obey formality rather than cure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character-based comedy can be built by exposing professions that prioritize form over function. Emphasize ritualistic speech, technical jargon, or obsessive adherence to form to show professional automatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical defects as comic overtones reinforcing professional or moral ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: A physical peculiarity (stammering, slowness, stuttering) often complements and amplifies the comic impression of intellectual or moral ossification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating comic characters, pairing a physical trait with an associated moral or intellectual failing produces coherent, resonant ridicule. Actors/writers may invent or exaggerate speech rhythms or physical tics to serve this function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person giving impression of being a thing (objectification)
rubrics_metrics.description: WE LAUGH EVERY TIME A PERSON GIVES US THE IMPRESSION OF BEING A THING (e.g., clowns whose bodies become like balls or wooden dummies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect arises from depersonalization and the visualization of persons as objects. Use physical staging, pacing, and imagery to transform human figures into thing-like entities (rolling, rigid postures, exaggerated collisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual suggestion / transition from vague to distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: A gradual passing from the dim and vague to the clear and distinct (slowly suggesting objectification or mechanicalness) is an effective method of comic suggestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build comic transformation by gradation—stepwise amplification, crescendo, or incremental hints—so the audience's imagination is led to accept an increasingly specific and absurd image (as in circus routines or hypnotic suggestion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rhythmic/literary devices to lull imagination into objectification
rubrics_metrics.description: By arranging rhythm, rhyme and assonance one can lull the imagination, rocking it 'between like and like' so as to prepare it to accept the suggested (often objectifying) image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In verse and prose, manipulate sound and rhythm to induce associative chaining in the reader's mind; this can stealthily deliver a toyed-with image (a doll, a thing) and increase comic resonance.
